title: Impure Products and Solubility of Salts
summary: Why real reactions give impure mixtures, how to separate and purify a salt, and how to read and use solubility curves — with worked examples, common mistakes and a Checkpoint-style quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Know that a reaction does not always give one pure product: often you get an impure mixture of products, and it must be separated. (8Cc.04)
Describe how the solubility of different salts changes with temperature, and read and use solubility graphs. (8Cc.05)

blocks.text: 2. Reactions often give a mixture, not one pure product

In Stage 7 you wrote word equations such as **magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen**. A word equation makes it look as if you finish with neat, separate products. In a real laboratory, what is left in the flask at the end is almost always a **mixture**. The product you want is **impure**, and you must separate and purify it.
Remember from the purity lesson: **purity** describes how much of the wanted chemical is in a sample. A sample that is 100 % one substance is **pure**. Anything else mixed in is an **impurity**.

rows: **1. More than one product is made.** Many reactions make two or three products at the same time.
copper carbonate + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water + carbon dioxide. The copper sulfate ends up **dissolved in the water**.
**2. Some reactant is left over.** Chemists often add one reactant **in excess** to make sure the other one is used up.
Excess black copper oxide powder stays at the bottom of the beaker after reacting with sulfuric acid.
**3. Side reactions happen.** Some of the reactants react in a different way and make unwanted substances.
When a fuel burns in too little oxygen it makes **carbon monoxide** and **soot** (carbon) as well as carbon dioxide and water.
**4. The starting materials were impure.** Impurities in the reactants are carried into the product.
Rock salt dug from the ground contains sand and clay, so salt made from it is impure until it is purified.

blocks.caption: What the beaker really contains after copper oxide (in excess) has reacted with sulfuric acid: a mixture, not pure copper sulfate.

blocks.text: 3. Getting a pure product: making copper sulfate crystals
Here is the standard way to make a pure, dry salt from an insoluble solid and an acid. Learn the **reason** for each step — Checkpoint often asks "Why did the student…?"

rows: Warm some dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker.
Warm acid reacts faster.
Add copper oxide a spatula at a time, stirring, until **some black powder stays** and will not react.
Adding **excess** copper oxide makes sure **all the acid is used up**, so no acid is left in the product.
**Filter** the mixture.
Removes the unreacted copper oxide (the **residue**). The blue copper sulfate solution goes through (the **filtrate**).
Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin until about half the water has gone, then leave it to cool.
The solution becomes **saturated**. As it cools, the salt is **less soluble**, so crystals form.
Filter off the crystals, wash with a little cold water and dry them between filter papers.
Removes the last bits of solution so the crystals are pure and dry.

blocks.caption: Copper sulfate as large blue crystals (top) and as a fine powder (bottom) — the same salt in both forms.
blocks.credit: Photo: W. Oelen / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.caption: Filtration separates an insoluble solid (residue) from a solution (filtrate).

blocks.text: **How can you tell if a product is pure?** A pure substance melts (and boils) at one **fixed temperature**. An impure substance melts over a **range** of temperatures, usually lower than the pure substance. Paper **chromatography** is another test: a pure substance gives only **one spot**.
**Percentage purity.** You can describe how pure a sample is with a percentage:

blocks.title: Formula
blocks.text: percentage purity = (mass of the wanted substance ÷ mass of the whole sample) × 100

blocks.text: 4. Solubility

When a salt dissolves in water, the salt is the **solute**, the water is the **solvent** and the mixture is a **solution**. If you keep adding salt and stirring, there comes a point when **no more will dissolve** — some solid stays at the bottom. The solution is now **saturated**.

The **solubility** of a substance is the **largest mass that will dissolve in 100 g of water at a stated temperature**. Its unit is **g per 100 g of water**. For example, the solubility of sodium chloride at 20 °C is about 36 g per 100 g of water: 100 g of water at 20 °C can dissolve 36 g of salt, but no more.

blocks.alt: White fibrous crystals of halite (rock salt)
blocks.caption: Halite is natural sodium chloride (rock salt); these crystals come from the Fayoum region of Egypt.
blocks.credit: Photo: Andrew Silver / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

blocks.title: Always give the temperature
blocks.text: A solubility value means nothing without a temperature, because **solubility changes with temperature**. "The solubility of potassium nitrate is 32 g" is incomplete; "32 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C" is correct.
5. How solubility changes with temperature
Scientists measure the solubility of a salt at several temperatures and plot a **solubility curve**. The table and graph show approximate values for three salts.

rows: potassium nitrate
copper sulfate
sodium chloride

blocks.caption: Solubility curves for three salts (approximate values, in g per 100 g of water).

blocks.text: What the graph tells you:

items: For **most salts, solubility increases as the temperature increases** — hot water dissolves more salt than cold water.

The **amount** of change is very different for different salts. Potassium nitrate rises very steeply (from 14 g at 0 °C to 167 g at 80 °C — more than ten times as much). Copper sulfate rises steadily.
Some salts hardly change. Sodium chloride (common salt) dissolves only about 2 g more at 80 °C than at 0 °C — its curve is almost flat.
A few salts are even slightly **less** soluble in hot water (lithium carbonate is one example), so never assume — always read the graph.
Where two curves **cross**, the two salts have the **same solubility** at that temperature (potassium nitrate and sodium chloride at about 23 °C).

blocks.text: **Using particles:** in hotter water the particles move faster and have more energy, so for most salts the water can break up and hold more of the salt's particles. You do not need to explain this in detail at Stage 8, but you must be able to **describe** the pattern from data.
6. Reading and using a solubility curve

items: **Solubility at a temperature:** go **up** from the temperature to the curve, then **across** to the solubility axis.
**Temperature for a given solubility:** go **across** from the solubility to the curve, then **down** to the temperature axis.
**Comparing salts:** at a given temperature, the **higher** curve is the **more soluble** salt.
**Crystals formed on cooling:** mass of crystals = solubility at the hot temperature − solubility at the cold temperature (for 100 g of water).
**Other masses of water:** scale up or down. 50 g of water dissolves **half** as much as 100 g; 200 g dissolves **twice** as much.

blocks.alt: Needle-shaped potassium nitrate crystals in a glass dish
blocks.caption: Needle-shaped crystals of potassium nitrate. Crystals like these form when a hot, saturated solution cools, because the salt is much less soluble in cold water.
blocks.credit: Photo: Adam Rędzikowski / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.title: قاعدة لازم تحفظها
items: الذوبانية = أكبر كتلة من الملح بتدوب في 100 جرام مية عند درجة حرارة معينة.
معظم الأملاح بتدوب أكتر لما المية تسخن، بس كل ملح بيتغيّر بمقدار مختلف (ملح الطعام تقريبًا ما بيتغيّرش).
لما محلول مشبع سخن يبرد ← الذوبانية تقل ← الملح الزيادة يطلع بلورات. كتلة البلورات = الذوبانية وهو سخن − الذوبانية وهو بارد.

blocks.text: 7. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — Sara makes magnesium sulfate by adding magnesium powder to dilute sulfuric acid until no more fizzing happens and some grey magnesium is left.
magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen
(a) Explain why the mixture in the beaker is not pure magnesium sulfate. [2] (b) Why did Sara add magnesium until some was left over? [1]

items: (a) The magnesium sulfate is **dissolved in water** (it is a solution) (1), and there is **unreacted magnesium** left over (1). (The hydrogen escapes as a gas.)
(b) So that **all the acid is used up** — no acid will be left mixed with the product.
**Common mistake:** writing "the hydrogen makes it impure". Hydrogen is a gas and bubbles away; the impurities that stay are the water and the leftover magnesium.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — A 40 g sample of salt made in a reaction contains 34 g of potassium chloride. Calculate its percentage purity. [2]

items: Percentage purity = (mass of potassium chloride ÷ mass of sample) × 100

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — Use the graph in section 5. (a) What is the solubility of potassium nitrate at 40 °C? [1] (b) Which salt is the most soluble at 10 °C? [1]

items: (a) Up from 40 °C to the potassium nitrate curve, then across: **61 g per 100 g of water**.
(b) At 10 °C the highest curve is the dotted line: **sodium chloride** (about 36 g). Potassium nitrate is only about 22 g at 10 °C.
**Common mistake:** in (b), choosing potassium nitrate because it is "the most soluble salt". It is only the most soluble **above** about 23 °C — always read the temperature you are asked about.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A saturated solution of potassium nitrate is made with 100 g of water at 60 °C. It is cooled to 20 °C. Calculate the mass of crystals that forms. [2]

items: At 60 °C, 100 g of water holds **106 g** of potassium nitrate.
At 20 °C it can hold only **32 g**.
Mass of crystals = 106 − 32 = **74 g** (1 mark for both readings, 1 mark for the answer).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — A saturated solution of copper sulfate is made with **50 g** of water at 80 °C and cooled to 20 °C. What mass of crystals forms? [2]

items: For 100 g of water: 55 g at 80 °C and 21 g at 20 °C, so 55 − 21 = 34 g of crystals.
50 g is half of 100 g, so the mass is halved: 34 ÷ 2 = **17 g**.
**Common mistake:** giving 34 g — the graph is always for **100 g** of water, so scale to the mass you are given.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Describe how the solubility of sodium chloride and potassium nitrate change between 0 °C and 80 °C. Use data in your answer. [2]

items: Potassium nitrate: solubility **increases a lot**, from 14 g to 167 g per 100 g of water (1).
Sodium chloride: solubility **increases only very slightly** / hardly changes, from 36 g to 38 g (1).
**Exam tip:** "Use data" means quote **numbers with units** from the table or graph. A pattern with no numbers usually loses a mark.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Thinking a word equation means you get pure products. In practice you usually get a mixture that must be separated.
Forgetting that the salt is **dissolved in water** — a solution is a mixture, not the pure salt.
Using evaporation to remove an insoluble solid. Insoluble solids are removed by **filtration**.
Giving a solubility with no temperature, or with the wrong unit (it is **g per 100 g of water**).
Saying "all salts dissolve more when hot". **Most** do, but by very different amounts, and a few dissolve less.
In cooling questions, reading only one value. Crystals = **hot value − cold value**, then scale for the mass of water.
Reading the wrong curve when graphs have several lines — trace the line with your finger or a ruler.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Explain why the product is impure** (2 marks): name the extra substances — water, leftover reactant, other products.
**Give the reason for a step** in a salt preparation: excess solid → all acid used up; filter → remove leftover solid; cool → crystals form.
**Read a solubility graph**: value at a temperature, temperature for a value, which salt is more soluble, where curves cross.
**Calculate crystals on cooling** — show both readings and the subtraction; scale for 50 g or 200 g of water.
**Describe the trend** with data ("as the temperature increases, the solubility increases from … to …").
**Plan** a solubility investigation: variables, saturated solution, repeats, safety (hot water, goggles).
Write units every time: g per 100 g of water, °C, %.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Impure products and solubility — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper first, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: A chemist says that a reaction has produced an **impure** product. What does this mean?
c: The product is mixed with other substances.
The product cannot be dissolved in water.
questions.e: **Impure** means the substance we want is **mixed with other substances** (impurities). Purity describes how much of the wanted chemical is in the mixture. Being a gas, being insoluble or giving out heat has nothing to do with purity.

questions.p:
Question 2
Amir makes copper sulfate. He adds black copper oxide powder to warm dilute sulfuric acid until no more will react. Some black powder is left at the bottom of the beaker.
copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water
questions.q: (a) What is in the beaker at the end of the reaction?
c: copper oxide dissolved in sulfuric acid
copper sulfate solution mixed with unreacted copper oxide
questions.e: The copper sulfate made is **dissolved in the water** (the reaction also makes water), and the **excess copper oxide** that did not react is left as a black solid. So the beaker holds a **mixture** — an impure product. Crystals only form later, after evaporating and cooling.

questions.p:
Question 2
Amir makes copper sulfate. He adds black copper oxide powder to warm dilute sulfuric acid until no more will react. Some black powder is left at the bottom of the beaker.
copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water
questions.q: (b) Name the method Amir should use to remove the black powder from the copper sulfate solution.
questions.e: **Filtration.** Copper oxide is insoluble, so it stays on the filter paper (the **residue**). The copper sulfate solution passes through (the **filtrate**). Evaporation would not work — the black powder would stay mixed with the crystals.

questions.q:
A sample of zinc sulfate made in a reaction has a mass of 25 g. Tests show that it contains 23 g of zinc sulfate; the rest is impurities.
Calculate the percentage purity of the sample. Show your working.
questions.e: percentage purity = (mass of the wanted substance ÷ mass of the whole sample) × 100 = (23 ÷ 25) × 100 = 0.92 × 100 = **92 %**. (1 mark for the working, 1 mark for the answer.) Common mistake: dividing the wrong way round, 25 ÷ 23 × 100 = 109 % — a purity can never be more than 100 %.

questions.q: Give **two** different reasons why a chemical reaction may not give a single pure product. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark each, any two: more than one product is made (e.g. a salt and water) / some reactant is left over (unreacted or in excess) / side reactions make unwanted products (e.g. carbon monoxide or soot when a fuel burns) / the reactants themselves contained impurities / the product is dissolved in water (a solution, not the pure substance). Do not accept 'the reaction went wrong' or 'the scientist made a mistake' without a chemical reason.
questions.e: Any two of: (1) the reaction makes **more than one product**, e.g. copper sulfate **and** water; (2) some **reactant is left over** (unreacted), e.g. excess copper oxide; (3) **side reactions** make unwanted substances, e.g. soot and carbon monoxide when a fuel burns in too little oxygen; (4) the **starting materials were impure**, so the impurities end up in the product.

questions.p:
Question 6
The graph shows the solubility of two salts, P and Q, at different temperatures.
questions.q: (a) What is the solubility of salt P at 40 °C?
questions.e: Go up from 40 °C on the temperature axis to the **solid** line (salt P), then across to the solubility axis: **45 g per 100 g of water**.

questions.p:
Question 6
The graph shows the solubility of two salts, P and Q, at different temperatures.
questions.q: (b) At what temperature is the solubility of salt P 65 g per 100 g of water?
questions.e: This time start on the **solubility** axis: go across from 65 to the curve for P, then down to the temperature axis: **60 °C**. Common mistake: reading across to the dashed line (salt Q), which never reaches 65.

questions.p:
Question 6
The graph shows the solubility of two salts, P and Q, at different temperatures.
questions.q: (c) Which statement about the two salts is correct?
c: Salt Q is more soluble than salt P at 10 °C.
Salt P is more soluble than salt Q at every temperature.
Both salts have the same solubility at 20 °C.
The solubility of salt Q rises faster than the solubility of salt P.
questions.e: At 10 °C the dashed line (Q, about 36–37 g) is **above** the solid line (P, about 25 g), so **Q is more soluble at 10 °C**. P is only more soluble above about 34 °C; at 20 °C P is 30 g and Q is 38 g (not the same); Q's line is much flatter, so its solubility rises **more slowly**.

questions.p:
Question 6
The graph shows the solubility of two salts, P and Q, at different temperatures.
questions.q: (d) At what temperature do salts P and Q have the same solubility?
questions.e: The two salts have the same solubility where the lines **cross**. Read straight down from the crossing point: about **34 °C** (both are about 40 g per 100 g of water there). Answers from 32 °C to 36 °C are accepted.

questions.p:
Question 6
The graph shows the solubility of two salts, P and Q, at different temperatures.
questions.q: (e) A saturated solution of salt P is made with 100 g of water at 80 °C. It is cooled to 20 °C. What mass of crystals of P forms? Show your working.
questions.e: At 80 °C, 100 g of water holds **90 g** of P. At 20 °C it can hold only **30 g**. The rest must come out of solution as crystals: 90 − 30 = **60 g**. (1 mark for reading both values, 1 mark for the subtraction.)

questions.p:
Question 6
The graph shows the solubility of two salts, P and Q, at different temperatures.
questions.q: (f) This time a saturated solution of salt P is made with only **50 g** of water at 60 °C, then cooled to 20 °C. What mass of crystals forms? Show your working.
questions.e: For 100 g of water: 65 g dissolves at 60 °C and 30 g at 20 °C, so 65 − 30 = 35 g of crystals. There is only 50 g of water — **half** of 100 g — so only half as much: 35 ÷ 2 = **17.5 g**. Common mistake: forgetting to halve, giving 35 g.

questions.p:
Question 6
The graph shows the solubility of two salts, P and Q, at different temperatures.
questions.q: (g) A student wants to make crystals by cooling a hot saturated solution. Which salt would give more crystals, and why?
c: salt Q, because its line is flatter
salt Q, because it is more soluble at 0 °C
salt P, because its solubility changes a lot with temperature
both the same, because they are both salts
questions.e: The mass of crystals depends on **how much the solubility falls** when the solution cools. P's solubility falls a lot (e.g. from 90 g at 80 °C to 20 g at 0 °C), but Q's hardly changes (47 g to 35 g). So **salt P** gives far more crystals on cooling. Salts like Q are better obtained by **evaporating** the water.

questions.p:
Question 6
The graph shows the solubility of two salts, P and Q, at different temperatures.
questions.q: (h) What is the largest mass of salt Q that will dissolve in **200 g** of water at 40 °C?
questions.e: At 40 °C the solubility of Q is 41 g per **100 g** of water. 200 g of water is twice as much, so it dissolves twice as much salt: 41 × 2 = **82 g**.

questions.q:
Plan an experiment to find how the solubility of potassium chloride changes with temperature.
In your answer, give the independent variable, the dependent variable, one control variable and how you will know when the solution is saturated. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: independent variable = temperature of the water AND dependent variable = mass of potassium chloride that dissolves (accept solubility). 1 mark: a correct control variable, e.g. same volume/mass of water / same amount of stirring / same salt. 1 mark: saturated when no more solid dissolves / some solid stays undissolved even after stirring. Also accept for credit (max 3): weigh the salt before and after to find the mass dissolved; use a water bath and thermometer to keep the temperature steady; repeat at several temperatures, e.g. 20, 40, 60 and 80 °C.
questions.e: Measure 100 g (100 cm³) of water into a beaker and heat it in a water bath to 20 °C, checking with a thermometer. Weigh a dish of potassium chloride. Add the salt a little at a time, stirring, until **some solid stays undissolved** however long you stir — now the solution is **saturated**. Reweigh the dish: the loss in mass is the mass that dissolved. Repeat at 40, 60 and 80 °C. **Independent variable:** temperature. **Dependent variable:** mass of salt that dissolves. **Control variables:** mass of water, amount of stirring, same salt. Repeat each temperature and calculate a mean to make the results more reliable.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Reactions often give an impure mixture: several products, leftover (excess) reactant, side reactions, or impure starting materials.
Separate and purify: filter off insoluble solids, evaporate and cool to crystallise, then wash and dry the crystals.
Percentage purity = (mass of wanted substance ÷ mass of sample) × 100.
Solubility = largest mass that dissolves in 100 g of water at a stated temperature; most salts dissolve more when hotter, by very different amounts.
Crystals on cooling = solubility (hot) − solubility (cold), scaled for the mass of water.
